Key Characteristics & Etiology: Biliary tree obstruction (CBD stone, stricture) with secondary bacterial infection (E. coli, Klebsiella).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Biliary stasis and elevated intraductal pressure lead to bacterial translocation into hepatic veins and systemic circulation.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Charcot's Triad (RUQ pain, fever with rigors, jaundice); Reynolds' Pentad (adds shock & altered mental status).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: USG shows dilated CBD (>6mm) and stones; LFTs show conjugated hyperbilirubinemia & ALP > 3x. Management: IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, urgent ERCP sphincterotomy/stenting.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Gallstones migrating from gallbladder into Common Bile Duct.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Impaction of calculus in CBD causing mechanical partial or complete extrahepatic biliary obstruction.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Biliary colic, fluctuating jaundice, dark urine, pale stools. Red Flag: Superadded infection leading to cholangitis.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: USG Abdomen (dilated CBD with hyperechoic stone); MRCP / ERCP. Management: ERCP stone extraction followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Gallstone impaction in cystic duct or Hartmann's pouch causing acute inflammation.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Luminal obstruction causes gallbladder distension, mucosal ischemia, chemical inflammation, and secondary bacterial infection.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Persistent RUQ pain radiating to right scapula, fever, nausea, vomiting, positive Murphy's sign.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: USG Abdomen (wall thickness >4mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's). Management: NBM, IV hydration, IV antibiotics, laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Ductal adenocarcinoma arising in the head or uncinate process of pancreas.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Insidious compression and occlusion of retropancreatic CBD, causing progressive extrahepatic cholestasis.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Painless, relentlessly progressive obstructive jaundice, severe pruritus, dark urine, clay stools, weight loss. Courvoisier's sign.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: LFTs (conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, ALP > 3-5x); CA 19-9; Multiphase CT (double-duct sign). Management: Whipple's procedure (Pancreaticoduodenectomy) or ERCP biliary stenting.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute inflammatory disease of pancreas; major causes are Gallstones (40%) and Alcohol (35%).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Intra-acinar zymogen activation causing pancreatic auto-digestion, tissue necrosis, microvascular thrombosis, and SIRS.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe epigastric pain radiating to back, severe vomiting, abdominal distension. Red Flag: Cullen's (periumbilical) & Grey Turner's (flank) ecchymosis.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Serum Lipase (>3x upper limit of normal); CT Abdomen. Management: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (Ringer's Lactate), analgesia, enteral nutrition.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Peripancreatic fluid collection persisting >4 weeks surrounded by fibrous/granulation tissue wall.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Disruption of pancreatic ductal system leaking pancreatic juice enclosed by adjacent retroperitoneal structures without epithelium.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Epigastric pain, early satiety, palpable epigastric mass, persistent elevation of serum amylase.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: CT Abdomen / EUS. Management: Watchful waiting if <6 cm/asymptomatic; Endoscopic cystogastrostomy or surgical drainage if symptomatic/growing.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Primary malignant liver tumor strongly linked to Chronic HBV/HCV, Cirrhosis, and Aflatoxin exposure.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Malignant transformation of hepatocytes driven by chronic inflammation and genomic instability; highly vascular tumor.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: RUQ pain, weight loss, anorexia, worsening ascites in known cirrhotic, palpable hepatic nodule.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP > 400 ng/mL); Triphasic CT (arterial hyperenhancement with venous washout). Management: BCLC staging; Resection, Liver Transplant, TACE, or Sorafenib/Atezolizumab.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Bacterial liver infection originating from ascending cholangitis, appendicitis, or portal pyemia (polymicrobial/E. coli).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Suppurative infection and liquefactive necrosis of liver parenchyma forming single or multiple fluid-filled cavities.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: High swinging fever with rigors, dull RUQ pain, tender hepatomegaly, mild jaundice.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: USG / CT Abdomen; Blood cultures; Pus aspirate. Management: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics + Percutaneous USG/CT-guided catheter drainage.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Infection by Entamoeba histolytica reaching liver via portal circulation from intestinal amoebiasis.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Trophozoites cause microvascular thrombosis and liquefactive necrosis of hepatocytes, forming 'anchovy-sauce' pus.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: High fever, painful tender hepatomegaly, right lower chest pain, intercostal tenderness.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Amoebic serology; USG Abdomen. Management: Oral/IV Metronidazole or Tinidazole for 10-14 days; aspiration if large or impending rupture.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Zoonotic infection caused by larval stage of tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Parasite forms slow-growing pericyst in liver with internal germinal layer producing daughter cysts and hydatid fluid.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Slowly enlarging painless RUQ mass, feeling of fullness. Red Flag: Anaphylaxis if cyst ruptures into peritoneum.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Echinococcus serology (ELISA); USG/CT ('water-lily sign', daughter cysts). Management: Oral Albendazole + PAIR procedure or surgical cystectomy.
